nary_nodes.label: Theft of Renaissance paintings in Messina
evidence: Criminals have once again targeted a small regional museum to steal priceless artworks on public display, this time in Messina, Sicily.
Local authorities say robbers bypassed alarm and security systems at the Regional Museum of Messina (MuMe), Italy, around 10:00 p.m. (2000 GMT) on Saturday evening...
Thieves were able to make off with several panels painted by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina...

nary_nodes.label: 1908 Messina earthquake destroying cultural heritage
evidence: The return of Antonello's painting to his hometown, went the argument, would have huge symbolic value for a city that lost most of its cultural heritage... on December 28, 1908 — when an earthquake flattened Messina...
The paintings stolen on Saturday belonged to an altarpiece installed at Messina's Monastero San Gregorio until it was destroyed in the 1908 quake.

nary_nodes.label: MuMe Director Marisa Mercurio on theft impact
evidence: "We are devastated by what happened. They were some of Antonello da Messina's most important and best-known works. It is a tremendous loss for the museum, the city, the community and the art world..."
"It is an extremely serious and significant loss..."

nary_nodes.label: Messina Mayor Federico Basile on theft timing
evidence: Messina Mayor Federico Basile called the theft "deeply reprehensible," saying it was "even more painful" for having taken place as the city celebrated the Assumption of the Virgin.

nary_nodes.label: 2026 Parma Foundation theft
evidence: Saturday's robbery comes just days after Italian authorities announced the recovery of three stolen artworks by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cezanne and Henri Matisse worth about €10 million.

evidence: Sicily's most famous art theft happened more than half a century ago, when unknown perpetrators broke into the church of the Oratorio di San Lorenzo in Palermo to cut Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio's 'Nativity with Saint Francis and Saint Lawrence' from its frame...

nary_nodes.label: Italian state purchases Antonello da Messina panel
evidence: Though the sum financial loss has not been made public — initial estimates range from €70-€80 million ($81-$92 million) — Antonello's market value increased considerably in March of this year when the Italian state laid out $14.9 million (€13 million) for the purchase of another panel that he painted around 1460.
